item.title: Extrinsic Curvature Estimation by Closest Point Projection of Rays
item.description: arXiv:2610.33943v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a parametrization-free framework for estimating the second fundamental form and the principal curvatures of a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The method uses the closest point projections of a few short random rays and recovers the curvature from the curves that these projections induce on the submanifold, without coordinate charts or local fitting. We analyze the geometry of the induced curves and characterize when they are geodesics. For hypersurfaces, these results give two algorithms with error bounds: a least squares reconstruction of the second fundamental form from the curvatures of the induced curves, and a direct estimate of all principal curvatures from the eigenvalues of a $d\times d$ matrix built from $d$ rays, which needs no normal information and costs $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ besides the projections. In higher codimension, we can also recover the second fundamental form one normal direction at a time. On point clouds, where the projection becomes a nearest neighbor query, we bound the additional error. Experiments confirm the predicted rates for hypersurfaces in up to $128$ dimensions, for surfaces of codimension up to $98$, and on point clouds, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in practice.
item.dc:creator: Liangchen Liu, Yen-Hsi Richard Tsai

item.title: A Pythagoras Tree Grown from a Dodecahedron
item.description: arXiv:2610.33975v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Pythagoras tree of A. E. Bosman (1942) is drawn with squares in the plane and, in the three-dimensional versions we know of, with cubes. This article documents a tree built instead from regular dodecahedra: each dodecahedron carries five smaller copies, one on each edge of a single pentagonal "crown" face, scaled by $g \approx 0.4346$ and twisted by $45^\circ$ about the edge. The construction first existed only as a pair of rendered images and two undocumented C++ programs. We recover its exact parameters from the original Blender scene, reformulate it as an iterated function system with condensation, and prove with a short computer-assisted argument that it never collides with itself: two of its dodecahedra overlap only when one is the parent of the other. A Pythagorean identity for the six face axes of the dodecahedron singles out the scale $1/\sqrt{5}$ and the twist $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$. With these values each child rests flat against a face of its parent, the five children together have exactly the parent's surface area, and the crown of the tree is a fractal of Hausdorff dimension exactly 2. Finally we ask whether the tree can grow on all twelve faces at once. A parity argument shows that at the artwork's proportions it cannot, but smaller scale factors admit certified clash-free all-faces trees.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Esteban P\'erez Ibarra

item.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for Euclidean $(k,z)$-Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.34373v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the optimal coreset size for Euclidean $(k,z)$-clustering, where $z\ge1$ is fixed. Huang, Li, and Wu (STOC 2024) proved a lower bound of $\Omega_z(k\varepsilon^{-z-2})$ for $\varepsilon\gtrsim_z k^{-1/(z+2)}$, matching the known upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors. For $0<\varepsilon<k^{-1/(z+2)}$, the upper bound $\widetilde O_z(k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2})$ remained unmatched. The previous lower bounds gave only $\Omega_z(\max\{k\varepsilon^{-2},k^{(2z+3)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-1}\})$. We close this gap by proving a matching lower bound throughout $0<\varepsilon<k^{-1/(z+2)}$, including arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$. Together with known bounds, this determines the optimal worst-case coreset size as $$ \widetilde\Theta_z\!\left(\min\left\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\right\}\right) $$ for every integer $k\ge1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. In particular, the bounds are $\widetilde\Theta(k^{4/3}\varepsilon^{-2})$ for $k$-median when $\varepsilon<k^{-1/3}$, and $\widetilde\Theta(k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ for $k$-means when $\varepsilon<k^{-1/4}$. Our construction uses projection levels to encode four-wise independent signs, allowing $k$ centers to detect omissions regardless of how the retained points are reweighted.
item.dc:creator: Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Jian Li, Baoduo Xu

item.title: DUET4D: Self-Corrective Coupled Guidance for Sparse-View 4D Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2610.35002v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sparse-view 4D reconstruction is highly under-constrained when only a few cameras are available. Generative priors can recover missing appearances, but video models are computationally impractical for iterative reconstruction, whereas single-view models produce temporally inconsistent pseudo-observations. Moreover, directly absorbing uncertain generative outputs into Gaussian optimization often creates redundant primitives and floating artifacts. To address these challenges, we propose DUET4D, a self-corrective coupled guidance framework for sparse-view 4D Gaussian splatting. The core of our approach is a self-corrective framework where the 4D representation guides generative prior for spatio-temporal consistent supervisions. We first construct sequential alignments from current Gaussian evidence to steer the latent restoration. Then we use Sequential Fidelity Resampling to lift generative supervisions into Gaussian space to selectively distinguish repeatedly supported primitives. The corrected representation then provides more reliable Gaussian evidence for the next restoration cycle. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET4D significantly improves rendering quality and rendering efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Beizhen Zhao, Nanjie Yao, Boyi Fu, Qingsong Yan, Haofan Ren, Kaiyong Zhao, Hao Wang

item.title: Query Complexity of Learning Axis-Aligned Partitions
item.description: arXiv:2610.35495v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work establishes the query complexity of learning high-dimensional boxes in the exact query learning setting. Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points, labeled by a collection of $k$ boxes: the label of each point in $X$ is determined by the unique box containing it. A learner aims to exactly recover the labels for every point in $X$ given access to a label oracle. We consider three increasingly-structured settings. In the most general setting, there are no conditions on the boxes, and they may overlap. We show that CAL (Cohn-Atlas-Ladner 1994), a classical active learning algorithm, is minimax-optimal with query complexity $\Theta(kd \log (n/kd))$. When the boxes are disjoint, we examine two regimes. In the large-$k$ regime, CAL remains minimax-optimal. For the constant-$k$ regime, an optimized variant of the Halving algorithm (Heged\"{u}s 1995) can beat CAL by a $\log(d)$ factor. Finally, in the most-structured settings, the boxes correspond to the leaves of a constant-sized decision tree. We prove a tight query complexity of $\Theta(d + \log n)$ that is additive in $d$ and $\log n$, generalizing a recent result (Black-Larsen-Mazumdar-Saha-So 2026) that establishes the query complexity of learning decision stumps.
item.dc:creator: Hadley Black, Arya Mazumdar, Barna Saha, Geelon So

item.title: Space-Efficient Approximate Spherical Range Counting in High Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2603.12106v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the following range searching problem in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces: given a finite set $P\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, where each $p\in P$ is assigned a weight $w_p$, and radius $r>0$, we need to preprocess $P$ into a data structure such that when a new query point $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$ arrives, the data structure reports the cumulative weight of points of $P$ within Euclidean distance $r$ from $q$. Solving the problem exactly seems to require space usage that is exponential to the dimension, a phenomenon known as the curse of dimensionality. Thus, we focus on approximate solutions where points up to $(1+\varepsilon)r$ away from $q$ may be taken into account, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an input parameter known during preprocessing. We build a data structure with near-linear space usage, and query time in $n^{1-\Theta(\varepsilon^4/\log(1/\varepsilon))}+t_q^{\varrho}\cdot n^{1-\varrho}$, for some $\varrho=\Theta(\varepsilon^2)$, where $t_q$ is the number of points of $P$ in the ambiguity zone, i.e., at distance between $r$ and $(1+\varepsilon)r$ from the query $q$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first data structure with efficient space usage (subquadratic or near-linear for any $\varepsilon>0$) and query time that remains sublinear for any sublinear $t_q$. We supplement our worst-case bounds with a query-driven preprocessing algorithm to build data structures that are well-adapted to the query distribution.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kalavas, Ioannis Psarros

item.title: Higher-order Persistence Diagrams
item.description: arXiv:2605.09866v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Persistent homology tracks when topological features appear and disappear across filtered data and represents the lifetime of each feature by a persistence interval. In multiple instance learning, when the instances in a bag use filtrations over the same ordered parameter space, we can compare relationships between persistence intervals across instances. No existing method is designed to aggregate collections of persistence diagrams in multiple instance learning into a single persistence diagram of implications between intervals. We introduce higher-order persistence diagrams to represent relationships between persistence intervals and recursively construct each higher-order persistence interval from a pair of lower-order persistence intervals. We then aggregate these relationships across the persistence diagrams in a bag. Explicit construction of this aggregate is computationally expensive, so we introduce harmonic aggregation to compute coordinates of the aggregate from the lower-order persistence diagrams without explicitly constructing it. Computing a harmonic aggregation coordinate has lower asymptotic computational complexity than explicitly constructing the aggregate. We evaluate harmonic aggregation against persistence landscapes, persistence images, and PersLay on random network model and real-world graph-classification benchmarks, and find that harmonic aggregation has the highest accuracy on the random network model benchmark and on most real-world data benchmarks. Source code is available at https://github.com/cfanning8/higher-order-PDs.
item.dc:creator: Charles Fanning, Mehmet Aktas

item.title: Query-Efficient Fixpoints of $\ell_p$-Contractions
item.description: arXiv:2503.16089v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that an $\epsilon$-approximate fixpoint of a map $f:[0,1]^d\rightarrow [0,1]^d$ can be found with $\mathcal{O}(d^2(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon} + \log\frac{1}{1-\lambda}))$ queries to $f$ if $f$ is $\lambda$-contracting with respect to an $\ell_p$-metric for some $p\in [1,\infty)\cup\{\infty\}$. This generalizes a recent result of Chen, Li, and Yannakakis [STOC'24] from the $\ell_\infty$-case to all $\ell_p$-metrics. Previously, all query upper bounds for $p\in [1,\infty) \setminus \{2\}$ were either exponential in $d$, $\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}$, or $\log\frac{1}{1-\lambda}$. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis also show how to ensure that all queries to $f$ lie on a discrete grid of limited granularity in the $\ell_\infty$-case. We provide such a rounding for the $\ell_1$-case, placing an appropriately defined version of the $\ell_1$-case in $\textsf{FP}^{dt}$. To prove our results, we introduce the notion of $\ell_p$-halfspaces and generalize the classical centerpoint theorem from discrete geometry: for any $p \in [1, \infty) \cup \{\infty\}$ and any mass distribution (or point set), we prove that there exists a centerpoint $c$ such that every $\ell_p$-halfspace defined by $c$ and a normal vector contains at least a $\frac{1}{d+1}$-fraction of the mass (or points).
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Haslebacher, Jonas Lill, Patrick Schnider, Simon Weber

item.title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2610.31719v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even for points in general position with integer coordinates. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, resolving the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. We reduce from MaxCut on permutation graphs by representing source vertices with classes of geometric edges, whose crossings encode source adjacencies. The complete target also contains every other edge between its points, and their freely chosen colours can affect the encoded cost. To control these interactions, we construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use program points to turn this reference into colour preferences on other edges. The optimum differs from a computable baseline plus the amplified minimum number of uncut source edges by an error small enough to distinguish consecutive source values. The reduction is deterministic, with polynomially many points and polynomial coordinate bit length.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Zhang
